Lab 17

Volcano

Shape a mountain, dig a crater, paint glowing lava down its sides, then fly a camera around it in Blender.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how 3D artists combine modelling, modifiers and materials to make a natural object look real.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer and a mouse with a scroll wheel (on a laptop trackpad, see this fix). This lab takes about four lessons. Save your file as Lab17_Volcano_YourName.blend.

You've got it when you can

  • use proportional editing and falloff to shape a mountain with a crater
  • use a Displace modifier and a texture to add rocky detail
  • build a material from nodes, including lava that glows
  • paint a mask and use it to mix two materials
  • explain why detail at three different sizes makes a model look real
  • keyframe a camera move and render it as a video

Why real things look real

Look closely at any real mountain and you'll find detail at every size: the overall shape, the lumps and ridges, and the gritty surface of the rock itself. Computer models look fake when one of those sizes is missing.

In this lab you'll add each size of detail with a different Blender tool, then add light. Switch the layers on one at a time and watch the cross-section of your volcano change.

Cross-section of your volcano

Each button is one layer of realism and the Blender tool that makes it.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Vertex
A single point on a 3D model. Edges join vertices; faces fill between edges.
Proportional editing
Moves the vertices near your selection too, so you pull smooth hills instead of spikes.
Falloff
The curve that decides how quickly that pull fades with distance.
Modifier
An effect stacked on an object that changes it without destroying the original mesh.
Texture
A pattern of numbers from black (0) to white (1) that other tools can read.
Node
One box in the Shader Editor. Wires carry numbers and colours from node to node.
Principled BSDF
Blender's all-in-one surface node: colour, shininess, bumps and glow.
Emission
Light that a surface gives out by itself, like a screen or hot lava.
Color Ramp
Turns a number from 0 to 1 into a colour, using colour stops you place.
Mask
A black-and-white map that says where one thing shows and where another does.
Fac or Factor
A number from 0 to 1 that controls how much of something you get. Older Blender calls it Fac, newer Blender calls it Factor.
Keyframe
A saved value at one frame. Blender fills in the frames between keyframes.
Interpolation
How Blender fills in those in-between frames. Bezier, the default, eases in and out. Linear moves at a constant speed.
Empty
An object with no shape that never renders: just a point in space for other objects to aim at or follow.
Constraint
A rule an object obeys automatically, such as "always point at that".
Parent
Linking one object to another so the child follows wherever the parent moves or turns.

Part 1

Shape the mountain

Tools: Edit Mode, Circle Select and Proportional Editing. Tick each step as you finish it.

Every step starts with a drawing of the part of Blender you’ll use. The orange numbers are the order to click or type. They are simplified drawings, not screenshots, so the colours and spacing in your Blender will differ a little, but the words and the positions match.

  1. Start fresh and save

    File › New › General. Click the cube, press X and choose Delete. Then File › Save As and name it Lab17_Volcano_YourName.blend.

    From now on, press Ctrl+S every few steps.

  2. Add a dense grid

    Add › Mesh › Grid. Straight away, open the Add Grid panel in the bottom-left corner of the viewport and set:

    X Subdivisions 200, Y Subdivisions 200, Size 20 m

    Why?

    A 200 × 200 grid has 40,401 vertices. Each one is a point you can push up or down, so more points means a smoother mountain and finer bumps later. It's the same reason you subdivided the cloth in Lab 15.

  3. Look down from above in Edit Mode

    Press Tab for Edit Mode. Click the blue Z circle on the navigation gizmo (top-right of the viewport), or press Numpad 7. Press Home so the grid fills the view, then Alt+A to deselect everything.

  4. Select the summit

    Press C for Circle Select. Scroll the mouse wheel (or press Numpad + / Numpad -) until the circle is about one-seventh of the grid's width (left picture below). Click once in the exact middle of the grid, then right-click to finish.

    Why a circle and not one vertex?

    Lifting a whole disc gives the mountain a small flat top. You need that flat top in Step 9 to dig a crater into — a single vertex would make a sharp point with nowhere to dig.

  5. Turn on Proportional Editing

    Press O (the letter). The target-shaped icon at the top of the viewport turns blue. Click the small arrow beside it and choose Sharp.

    Why Sharp?

    Proportional editing also drags the vertices around your selection, less and less the further away they are. The falloff curve decides the shape of that fade, so it decides what kind of volcano you get. Try each falloff below.

Falloff explorer

These are Blender's real falloff curves. The settings match the Move panel you'll use in Step 7.

  1. Pull the mountain up

    Press G, then Z, type 4.5 and press Enter. Don't judge it yet. The spread is probably wrong, and you'll fix it next.

  2. Set the spread

    Open the Move panel in the bottom-left corner. Check that Proportional Falloff says Sharp, then set Proportional Size to 8 m. Hold the middle mouse button and drag to orbit around your mountain.

    The Move panel disappears as soon as you do anything else. If it's gone, press F9 to bring it back, or press Ctrl+Z and repeat Step 6.

  3. Select the crater area

    Look from above again (Z on the gizmo) and press Alt+A. Scroll to zoom in on the summit first, then press C. Scroll (or Numpad + / Numpad -) until the circle is about two-thirds the width of the flat top (right picture above), click the middle once and right-click.

  4. Predict, then dig

    Change the falloff (arrow beside the proportional icon) to Smooth.

    Predict first: Proportional Size is still 8 m. When you push the crater down, what will happen to the rest of the mountain? Say it to the person next to you.

    Now press G, Z, type -1.5, Enter. Then, in the Move panel, set Proportional Size to 0.8 m.

    What just happened?

    With an 8 m circle of influence, the whole mountain sank along with the crater. Shrinking the size to 0.8 m keeps the dig inside the flat top, and the untouched edge becomes the crater's rim.

  5. Smooth it and save

    Press Tab to go back to Object Mode. Right-click the volcano and choose Shade Smooth. Save with Ctrl+S.

Part 2

Make it rugged

Tools: Displace modifier and a Clouds texture. This is the medium-sized detail.

  1. Add a Displace modifier

    In the Properties panel, open the Modifiers tab (blue wrench), then Add Modifier › Deform › Displace. Nothing changes yet, because it needs a texture to read.

  2. Give it a texture

    In the Displace modifier, click New. Open the Texture tab (the red-and-white chequered icon at the bottom of the tab column) and change Type to Clouds.

    Why?

    A texture is a black-and-white pattern. Displace pushes the surface out where the texture is white and in where it's black, like pressing a bumpy stamp into clay.

  3. Make the clouds rocky

    In the Clouds settings set Type Hard, Size 1.5 and Depth 6.

    What do these do?

    Size is how wide each bump is. Depth is how many layers of smaller bumps are stacked on top. Hard makes sharp creases like eroded rock instead of soft blobs.

  4. Set how tall the bumps are

    Go back to the Modifiers tab and set the Displace Strength to 0.8. Save.

    Why 0.8?

    Strength is how tall the bumps are. Above about 1.5 the volcano starts to look like a pile of crumbs, and the crater disappears.

End of lesson 1. Save and stop here.

Part 3

Rock and lava materials

Tools: Shader Editor, Principled BSDF, Noise Texture, Bump and Color Ramp. This is where the small detail and the glow come from.

This is the node setup you'll have at the end of Part 4. Come back to it whenever you're unsure what plugs into what. The coloured dots match Blender's: yellow carries colour, grey a number, purple a direction and green a shader.

Adding nodes: hover over the Shader Editor, press Shift+A and just start typing the node's name, then press Enter. To connect two nodes, drag from a dot on one to a dot on the other, like this:

  1. Open the Shading workspace

    Click the Shading tab along the top of Blender. With the volcano selected, click New in the Shader Editor (the bottom half). A Principled BSDF appears, already connected to a Material Output. Double-click the material's name and call it Volcano.

  2. Make the rock dark and dull

    On the Principled BSDF, click Base Color and type Hex 4B4642. Set Roughness to 0.9.

    Why?

    Volcanic rock (basalt) is dark grey-brown and doesn't shine. High roughness spreads light out so there are no glossy highlights.

  3. Add tiny rock grain

    Add a Noise Texture and a Bump node. Connect Noise Fac (some versions label it Factor) to Bump Height, then Bump Normal to the Principled BSDF's Normal. Set:

    Noise Scale 120, Detail 10, Bump Strength 0.5

    Why?

    Bump fakes tiny dents using light and shadow without moving any vertices. It's the third and smallest size of detail, and it's cheap for the computer.

  4. Add a second Principled BSDF

    Add another Principled BSDF and drag it below the first. This one becomes the lava. Leave the first one alone — it's your rock.

  5. Add the lava pattern

    Add another Noise Texture. Change its 3D dropdown to 4D, then set Scale 30 and Detail 8.

    Why 4D?

    4D adds a value called W. Changing W makes the pattern slowly churn, as if the lava is moving. You'll animate it in Part 5.

  6. Colour it with a Color Ramp

    Add a Color Ramp and connect the new Noise Fac to the ramp's Fac. Then set up three colour stops:

    Click the left stop: Pos 0.45, keep it black.
    Click the right stop: Pos 0.65, colour Hex FFB52E.
    Click + to add a stop: Pos 0.55, colour Hex FF4D00.

    Why?

    The noise is just grey numbers from 0 to 1. The ramp turns low numbers into black crust and high numbers into yellow-hot lava. Drag the stops below to see how each one changes the look.

Lava playground

A copy of your lava nodes: Noise Texture into Color Ramp into Emission. Drag the stops, then switch on W to see what Part 5 does.

Selected stop: middlePos 0.55Hex FF4D00
W = 0.00

  1. Make it glow

    On the lava Principled BSDF, click the word Emission to open that section. Connect the Color Ramp's Color to the lava BSDF's Base Color, and connect it again to Emission Color. Set Emission Strength to 4.

    Why?

    Emission means the surface gives out its own light. Real lava is around 1,000 °C — hot enough to glow. Black parts of the ramp give out no light, so the crust stays dark.

  2. Test the lava

    Drag from the lava BSDF's BSDF output to the Material Output's Surface. Your whole volcano turns to lava! That's expected: Part 4 puts the lava only where you want it.

End of lesson 2. Save and stop here.

Part 4

Paint the lava flows

Tools: Vertex Paint, Color Attribute and Mix Shader.

You have two materials now: rock and lava. A mask decides which one shows where. It's a black-and-white map painted onto the volcano. Black means rock, white means lava. Try painting one here before you do it in Blender.

Mask painter

The volcano from directly above. Paint with your mouse or finger. Start in the crater, then run flows downhill.

Switch to The mask to see what Blender actually stores: just black and white. The Mix Shader reads black as 0 (rock) and white as 1 (lava).

  1. Switch to Vertex Paint

    Click the Layout tab at the top. With the volcano selected, open the mode dropdown in the top-left (it says Object Mode) and choose Vertex Paint. The volcano turns white.

    Why white?

    Blender has just created a colour layer that stores a colour on every vertex. It starts white, and it's saved inside your .blend file.

  2. Turn it all black

    Paint › Invert. The whole volcano goes black, which means all rock.

  3. Set up the brush

    In the bar along the top, check the colour swatch is white (click it and drag the brightness up). Set Strength to 1. Press F, move the mouse to resize the brush and click to confirm. Start with a brush about as wide as your finger on the screen.

  4. Paint the lava

    Fill the crater floor with white. Then paint 3 to 5 flows starting at the rim. Let each one run downhill, following the valleys and bending around bumps. Make them thinner near the top and wider near the bottom. Ctrl+Z undoes a stroke.

    Why follow the valleys?

    Lava is a liquid, so gravity pulls it into the lowest channels. Flows that cut straight across ridges look fake straight away.

  5. Hook the mask up

    Go to the Shading tab. Add a Color Attribute node and a Mix Shader. Then connect:

    Color Attribute Color → Mix Shader Fac (Factor in some versions)
    Rock BSDF → Mix Shader top Shader socket
    Lava BSDF → Mix Shader bottom Shader socket
    Mix Shader → Material Output Surface

    If the Color Attribute node's dropdown is empty, choose your colour layer from it.

    Why does this work?

    The Mix Shader uses the top shader when Fac is 0 (black) and the bottom shader when Fac is 1 (white). The soft grey edges of your brush strokes blend the two, like lava cooling into rock.

Part 5

Light it and animate

Tools: World, Sun light, keyframes and a still render. The camera gets its own part next.

  1. Make it night

    In the Properties panel open the World tab (red globe). Set Color to Hex 262B3D and Strength to 1. Press Z over the viewport and choose Rendered to see it.

  2. Set a low, warm sun

    Click the Light in the Outliner (top-right list). In the Light tab (green bulb) choose Sun, Strength 3, Color Hex FFEBD9. Then in the Object tab (orange square) set Rotation X 68°, Y 0°, Z 120°.

    The moment you pick Sun, Strength shows 1000 and the view goes almost white. That's normal: a sun is measured differently from a bulb. Type 3 and it settles down.

    Why low?

    A low sun throws long shadows, which shows off every bump you added in Part 2. A dark sky makes the lava look brighter by contrast.

  3. Frame your shot

    Orbit the viewport to a low, dramatic angle with the volcano filling most of the screen. Then View › Align View › Align Active Camera to View (Ctrl+Alt+Numpad 0).

  4. Animate the lava

    In the Shading tab, hover over the Shader Editor and press Shift+← to go to frame 1. Hover over W on the lava Noise Texture and press I. The field turns yellow, which means it's keyframed.

    Press Shift+→ to jump to frame 250. Set W to 3, hover over it and press I again. Press Space to play and Space again to stop.

    Why does it move?

    You saved W = 0 at frame 1 and W = 3 at frame 250. Blender fills in every frame between, so W creeps upward and the crust pattern churns. That's what the Animate W button did in the playground.

  5. Render and save

    Press F12. When the render finishes, choose Image › Save As in the render window and save a PNG named Lab17_Volcano_YourName.png. Save your .blend too. This still is one of the three files you'll hand in.

    EEVEE renders in seconds. Cycles (Render tab › Render Engine) lets the lava light up the rock more realistically, but it's much slower.

End of lesson 3. Save and stop here.

Part 6

Fly the camera

Tools: Camera, Empty, Track To constraint, Parent, keyframes and Render Animation. This part turns your render into a movie.

A movie camera does three things: it sits somewhere, it points at something, and it moves. In Blender the camera is just another object, so you already know how to do all three. You'll move it with numbers, aim it with a constraint, and keyframe it exactly like you keyframed W.

Two keyframes are all a camera move needs: one for where it starts and one for where it ends. Blender works out every frame in between. Start with the widget below to get a feel for where a camera sits and what it sees.

Where is the camera, and what does it see?

The left view is your Blender viewport (drag it to orbit, like the middle mouse button). The right view is what the camera sees when you press Numpad 0. The orange cross is the Target you'll add in Step 35; the thin line is the camera's aim.

Your viewport — drag to orbit
What the camera sees

This widget needs WebGL, which your browser has switched off. The steps below still work without it.

  1. Give the volcano some ground

    Right now the world ends at the edge of your grid, which looks odd in a wide shot. In Object Mode: Add › Mesh › Plane, then in the Add Plane panel (bottom-left) set Size 200 m. Press G Z, type -0.3, Enter so it sits just under the bumpy edge of the grid.

    With the plane selected, open the Material tab (the red sphere at the bottom of the tab column), click New, and set Base Color Hex 4B4642, Roughness 0.9. Same rock, no lava.

    Why 200 m?

    A floor ten times wider than the grid lets the camera start a long way back without the edge of the world showing. Big, dark and boring is exactly what you want from ground.

  2. Look through the camera

    Hover over the 3D viewport and press Numpad 0. You're now looking through the Camera that has been in your scene since Step 1. The bright rectangle is the frame: only what's inside it ends up in a render. Everything outside is dimmed. Press Numpad 0 again to go back to your free view.

    No numpad? Click the small camera icon under the navigation gizmo (top-right of the viewport), or use View › Cameras › Active Camera.

    Why bother?

    In a movie, what the camera sees is all that exists. Get used to flicking in and out of camera view: free view to move things, camera view to judge the shot.

  3. Add a Target in the crater

    Leave camera view (Numpad 0). Add › Empty › Plain Axes. Press N to open the sidebar, click its Item tab, and set Location X 0, Y 0, Z 3. That's the middle of the crater floor. Press F2, type Target, Enter.

    What's an Empty?

    An object with no shape. It never shows up in a render. It's just a point in space with a position and a rotation that other objects can use. Ours marks the spot the camera should always look at.

  4. Make the camera always look at the Target

    Click Camera in the Outliner. In the Properties panel open the Constraints tab (the chain-link icon, just below the orange Object square). Add Object Constraint › Track To. Click the empty Target field and pick Target (your empty) from the list. Check that it says Track Axis -Z and Up Y (that's the default). Press Numpad 0: the crater is now in the middle of the frame.

    Why a constraint?

    A constraint is a rule an object obeys automatically. Track To means "always point your -Z axis at that object", and a camera looks down its own -Z axis. From now on you can put the camera anywhere and it stays aimed at the crater. Switch Track To off in the widget above and move the camera: that drifting is what you'd have to fix by hand otherwise.

  5. Frame 1: type the start position

    Press Shift+← to go to frame 1 (the number is in the Timeline along the bottom of the Layout workspace). With the Camera selected, in the sidebar's Item tab set Location X 26, Y -22, Z 11. Leave Rotation alone: the constraint owns it now.

    Predict first: the camera is now about 35 m from the Target and 8 m above it. Will you be able to see the crater floor? Press Numpad 0 and check.
    Why these numbers?

    35 m away with a 50 mm lens shows about 25 m of ground, so the whole 19 m volcano fits with some sky above it: a wide "establishing shot". And no, you can't see the floor: from this low the near rim hides it. Keep that in mind for the end of the move.

  6. Save it as a keyframe

    Hover the mouse over the Location X box in the sidebar and press I. All three Location boxes turn yellow, and a yellow diamond appears at frame 1 in the Timeline. That's a keyframe: "at frame 1, be here". It's the same thing you did to W in Step 31.

    Yellow: keyframe on this frame Green: animated, in between keyframes Orange: you changed it but haven't pressed I

    Orange is the trap. If you change a number and move to another frame without pressing I, Blender throws the change away.

  7. Frame 250: type the end position and keyframe it

    Press Shift+→ to jump to frame 250. Set Location X 8, Y -7, Z 17. The boxes go orange. Hover over them and press I so they turn yellow again. The Timeline now shows two diamonds.

    Why end up high?

    The end position is closer and much higher, so the camera looks down over the rim into the glowing crater. The start hides the floor and the end reveals it: a move with a payoff.

  8. Play it

    Press Numpad 0 so you're looking through the camera, then Space. The camera glides in from the wide shot and rises until you're looking into the crater while the lava churns. Space again stops it. You can also drag the blue playhead in the Timeline to scrub through the move.

    Notice it starts gently and slows to a stop. Blender eases every keyframe by default (that's the Bezier button in the widget below). Real camera operators move like that too.

    Nothing happens? See the camera doesn't move.

Keyframes make it move

A copy of your camera animation. Pick a move, then scrub or play the timeline. The boxes underneath are the sidebar values: yellow means "a keyframe is here", green means "Blender worked this out in between".

Your viewport — drag to orbit
What the camera sees

This widget needs WebGL, which your browser has switched off. The steps still work without it.

Frame 1 / 250
Camera › Location
XLocation X26 m
YLocation Y-22 m
ZLocation Z11 m
Target › Rotation
ZRotation Z0°

Camera is not parented to the Target.

  1. Tie the camera to the Target

    Now for the orbit. Go back to frame 1 (Shift+←). In the Outliner click Camera, then Ctrl+click Target, so both are selected and Target is the brighter one. Hover over the 3D viewport, press Ctrl+P and choose Object. Nothing visible changes yet.

    What did that do?

    The camera is now the Target's child. Children follow their parent: when the Target turns, the camera swings around it like a ball on a string, staying the same distance away. Your location keyframes still work; they're just measured from the Target now.

    Do this at frame 1 while the Target's Rotation Z is still 0°. Parent first, keyframe the Target second.

  2. Spin the Target

    Click Target in the Outliner. At frame 1, check the sidebar says Rotation Z 0°, hover over it and press I. Jump to frame 250 (Shift+→), set Rotation Z to 90, hover and press I. Go into camera view and press Space: the camera now sweeps a quarter of the way around the volcano as it flies in. A drone shot.

    Why does the camera move when I only keyframed the Target?

    Because it's parented. The Target turns 90° between the keyframes, and the camera comes along for the ride. Track To keeps it pointed at the crater the whole way. Try 180 for a half circle: same length of movie, twice the speed.

  3. Set up the video output

    Open the Output tab (the printer icon). Under Format set Resolution X 1920, Y 1080 and % to 50. Check Frame Rate is 24 fps and Frame Start 1, End 250: that's about 10 seconds of video.

    Under Output, click the folder icon and pick a folder you can find again (your Lab 17 folder). Set File Format to FFmpeg Video. Under Encoding set Container MPEG-4 and Video Codec H.264.

    Why 50%?

    960 × 540 has a quarter of the pixels of 1080p, so it renders about four times faster and still looks fine on a screen. MPEG-4 with H.264 is the ordinary .mp4 that plays anywhere.

  4. Preview it the fast way

    Put the viewport in Rendered shading (Z) and camera view (Numpad 0). Then View › Viewport Render Animation. Blender grabs each frame straight from the viewport, which is much faster than a real render. When it finishes, Render › View Animation (Ctrl+F11) plays your movie. Not happy with the move? Change the keyframes and run it again.

    If the grid or the Target's axes show up in the preview, switch off Overlays (the two-circles icon at the top of the viewport) and run it again.

  5. Render the movie and save

    Render › Render Animation (Ctrl+F12). A window shows each frame as it finishes. 250 frames at half size takes a few minutes in EEVEE, so start it and do the quiz while you wait. The finished file is in your output folder, named after its frame range, something like 0001-0250.mp4. Rename it Lab17_Volcano_YourName.mp4, then save your .blend with Ctrl+S.

    Too slow? In the Render tab (camera-back icon), under Sampling, drop Render from 64 to 16. See rendering takes forever.

End of lesson 4. That's the whole lab.

Finished early?

Pick one. Each makes your volcano more realistic in a different way.

Make it erupt with a smoke plume

This uses a domain, exactly like the water in Lab 16: smoke can only exist inside the domain box.

  1. Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. In its panel set Radius 0.5 m. Press G Z and lift it into the crater.
  2. With the sphere selected: Object › Quick Effects › Quick Smoke. A box appears. That's the domain.
  3. Select the box. Press S 2 Enter to double its size, then G Z 3 Enter to give the smoke headroom.
  4. In the Physics tab, set Resolution Divisions to 64.
  5. Select the sphere. In the Object tab, under Visibility › Show In, untick Renders.
  6. Select the box. In the Material tab, set the Principled Volume Color to a dark ash grey (Hex 3A3633).
  7. Press Space. The first play is slow because Blender is calculating every frame. Smoke shows in Material Preview or Rendered view.
Zoom the lens as the camera flies (the Vertigo shot)

A camera's lens can be keyframed like anything else. Fly in while zooming out and the volcano stays about the same size while the ground rushes past: the dizzy "Vertigo" effect from the movies.

  1. Select the Camera and open its Object Data tab (the green camera icon).
  2. At frame 1 set Focal Length to 70 mm, hover over it and press I.
  3. At frame 250 set it to 35 mm and press I again.
  4. Play it in camera view. The camera ends twice as close with a lens half as long, so the mountain barely changes size while everything around it stretches.
Carve gullies with Sculpt Mode

Real volcanoes have deep channels running down from the top where rain and lava have worn the rock away.

  1. Switch the mode dropdown to Sculpt Mode and pick the Draw brush.
  2. Hold Ctrl and drag from the rim downhill to dig a gully. Do this 6 to 10 times, spread around the mountain.
  3. Hold Shift and drag to smooth any mistakes.
  4. Back in Vertex Paint, move your lava flows into the new gullies.
Volcano types: build a cinder cone and a shield volcano

Add two more grids next to your volcano (move them sideways with G X). Repeat Steps 3 to 7 with different falloffs:

  1. Cinder cone: Linear falloff, Move Z 3, Proportional Size 5 m.
  2. Shield volcano: Root falloff, Move Z 2, Proportional Size 9 m.

Render all three side by side and label which is which. Use the Falloff explorer in Part 1 to check your thinking.

Something's not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

Pressing G Z moves the whole grid, not a mountain

Proportional editing is off. Press O (the icon turns blue) and try again. Also check that only the small middle disc is selected: Alt+A, then redo Step 4.

My mountain is a thin spike or a giant block

A spike means Proportional Size is too small. A block with cliff sides means the falloff is Constant. Fix both in the Move panel (Step 7).

The Move panel disappeared

It only lasts until your next action. Press F9 to reopen it. If that does nothing, press Ctrl+Z, then do the move again — the panel comes back.

I can't orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured axis gizmo in the top-right of the viewport. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

Displace moved everything but there are no bumps

The texture type is still Image or Movie. Open the Texture tab and change Type to Clouds (Step 12).

It looks spiky, blocky or like crumbs

Strength is too high or Size is too small. Use Strength 0.8 and Size 1.5. Did you do Shade Smooth in Step 10?

The lava doesn't glow

Your viewport is in Solid view: press Z and choose Material Preview or Rendered. Then check the lava BSDF's Emission section: the Color Ramp must be plugged into Emission Color, and Emission Strength must be 4.

The whole volcano is still lava after Step 27

Either the lava BSDF is still plugged straight into the Material Output (it should go through the Mix Shader), or your mask is all white. In Vertex Paint, use Paint › Invert and repaint the flows.

I painted flows but no lava shows

Check three things: the Color Attribute's Color goes into the Mix Shader's Fac; the right colour layer is picked in the Color Attribute dropdown; and lava is in the bottom Shader socket, not the top.

My brush paints black

The brush colour is black. Click the colour swatch in the top bar and drag the brightness to white.

The lava doesn't move when I press Space

Check the lava Noise Texture is set to 4D, and that W has a keyframe at frame 1 (W = 0) and another at frame 250 (W = 3). Use ↑ and ↓ to jump between keyframes and check.

I don't have a numpad

Click the camera icon under the navigation gizmo (top-right of the viewport) to look through the camera, or use View › Cameras › Active Camera. For the top view use the gizmo's Z. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate Numpad, and the number keys along the top of the keyboard do the numpad's job.

The camera points the wrong way

Select the Camera and open the Constraints tab. The Track To constraint must have Target in its Target box, Track Axis -Z and Up Y. If the constraint is missing, redo Step 36. If the Target itself is not at (0, 0, 3), select it and type those numbers in the sidebar.

The camera doesn't move when I play

Look at the Location boxes in the sidebar with the Camera selected. Orange means you typed a number but never pressed I, so Blender threw it away. Go to frame 1, type the start numbers, press I; go to frame 250, type the end numbers, press I. You should see two diamonds in the Timeline. Also check you're playing in camera view (Numpad 0): in free view the camera moves but your viewpoint doesn't.

The camera jumps or spirals when I parent it

The Target already had rotation keyframes when you parented. Fix: select the Target, hover over Rotation in the sidebar and choose right-click › Clear Keyframes. Set Rotation Z to 0 at frame 1. Select the Camera and Object › Parent › Clear Parent (Alt+P). Then redo Steps 41 and 42 in that order.

I can't find the video file

Blender saves it in the folder set in the Output tab. If you never changed it, that's C:\tmp\ on Windows or /tmp/ on Mac and Linux. The file is named after its frame range, like 0001-0250.mp4. If there are hundreds of PNG files instead, File Format was still PNG: set it to FFmpeg Video and render again.

Rendering the animation takes forever

Three things, in order: Output tab, Resolution % to 50. Render tab, Sampling, Render samples to 16. And for checking the move, use View › Viewport Render Animation instead of a full render. 250 frames at those settings should take a few minutes, not an hour.

Blender is really slow

Stay in Solid view while modelling and only switch to Material Preview when you need to see colours. Close other programs. If it's still slow, start again with 120 subdivisions in Step 2 instead of 200.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You'll find out straight away whether you're right.

1Why does the grid need 200 × 200 subdivisions?

Right. Every vertex is a point that can move, so more vertices means more detail.

Not quite. More vertices means the shape and the Displace bumps have enough points to show fine detail.

2Which falloff gives a stratovolcano's shape: steep at the top and gentle at the bottom?

Right. Sharp drops away quickly near the selection and then flattens out, giving a concave slope like Mount Fuji's.

Not quite. Sharp gives the concave slope. Linear makes straight sides (a cinder cone) and Sphere makes a dome.

3In the Displace modifier, what does Strength change?

Right. Strength is height. The texture's Size is width, and Depth is the number of layers.

Not quite. Strength is how tall the bumps are. Size sets how wide they are, and Depth sets how many layers.

4What makes the lava look like it's glowing?

Right. Emission makes the surface give out its own light.

Not quite. The glow comes from Emission: the ramp's colours go into Emission Color, and Emission Strength sets how bright.

5A white part of your mask sends Fac = 1 into the Mix Shader. Which shader shows there?

Right. Fac 1 uses the bottom shader, and Fac 0 uses the top one.

Not quite. Fac 1 (white) uses the bottom socket, which is the lava. Fac 0 (black) uses the top socket, which is the rock.

6Why did you switch the lava Noise Texture to 4D?

Right. Keyframing W from 0 to 3 makes the crust pattern churn over time.

Not quite. 4D adds the W value. Keyframing W from 0 to 3 is what makes the lava move.

7You keyframed the camera at frame 1 and frame 250. What does Blender do at frame 125?

Right. That's interpolation: Blender fills in every frame between two keyframes.

Not quite. Blender interpolates: at frame 125 the camera is part-way along the path between the two keyframes, without you typing anything.

8Why did the camera orbit the volcano when you only keyframed the Target's rotation?

Right. A child follows its parent like a ball on a string, and Track To keeps it aimed at the crater on the way round.

Not quite. Parenting is what moves it: the camera is the Target's child, so when the Target turns the camera swings around it. Track To only controls where the camera points.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

Which step made the biggest difference to how real your volcano looks, and why? If you had to turn your stratovolcano into a shield volcano, which step would you change? And which felt more like a film, the straight fly-in or the orbit? Why?

Upload to SEQTA — Lab 17

Upload three files: Lab17_Volcano_YourName.blend, your still render Lab17_Volcano_YourName.png and your movie Lab17_Volcano_YourName.mp4. Your .blend should include the crater, the Displace modifier, the rock and lava material, painted lava flows, the animated W value and the camera keyframes. Bonus marks for one of the extensions.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

About four lessons. Lesson 1: Today, the big idea and Parts 1–2. Lesson 2: Part 3. Lesson 3: Parts 4–5. Lesson 4: Part 6, the quiz and submission; have students start the final render before the quiz so it finishes while they work. The stop markers on the page match this split. Fast finishers move to the extensions.

Before this lab

Students should be able to navigate the viewport and switch between Object and Edit Mode. Lab 15 introduced subdividing and modifiers, and Lab 16 introduced the domain, which the smoke extension reuses.

Tested values

Every value was checked in Blender 5.0.1, and the checkpoint images were rendered from these exact steps. Menu names match Blender 4.2 LTS onwards. The Shift+A node categories moved between versions, so the steps use search instead of menu paths. The smoke extension couldn't be test-rendered, so it follows Blender's standard Quick Smoke setup. Part 6 was rebuilt from the steps in Blender 4.2.23 LTS and its checkpoint images are Cycles renders of that scene (EEVEE output looks the same but with less light spilling from the lava onto the rock); the Track To defaults (-Z, Y), the 200 m plane, the camera positions and the parented orbit were all verified there. Note that switching the default Point light to Sun keeps its 1000 W energy, which is why Step 29 now warns about the white-out.

Where students usually get stuck

The Move panel vanishing before they set Proportional Size (Ctrl+Z and repeat). The Principled BSDF's Emission section being collapsed. Vertex Paint starting white, which Step 24 handles. Laptops without a middle mouse button. Material Preview ignoring the World colour, so Step 28 uses Rendered view. In Part 6: changing the end position at frame 250 and forgetting to press I (orange fields), keyframing the Target before parenting the camera to it, no numpad on laptops (the troubleshooting entry covers it), and the output folder defaulting to /tmp. Viewport Render Animation is the fast way to check a move before committing to a full render.
